newsitem.title: UK: Stg skids off highs as UK's Clarke sounds alarm.
newsitem.headline: Stg skids off highs as UK's Clarke sounds alarm.

text.p: Sterling lurched downhill in late European trading on Tuesday, falling back from four-year highs after Finance Minister Kenneth Clarke said British business was starting to fret about the pound's exchange rate.
"At the moment our currency is strengthening very strongly and large numbers of British industries are beginning to get worried that we might get too strong," Clarke told parliament.

Sterling's overnight surge to 2.6370 German marks, its best level since it crashed out of Europe's exchange rate mechanism in September 1992, was the latest leg in a sharp rally which has squeezed British competitiveness by making exports more expensive and cheapening imports.
But by the early evening it had slumped almost nine pfennigs from its peak, trading at 2.5470 marks compared to Monday's European close of 2.5977.
Against the dollar, it was more than four cents down on the day, near one-month lows at $1.6375 versus late Monday's $1.6830.
Leading British industrialists have been complaining recently about the damage that a strong pound could inflict on their competitiveness.
Gordon Campbell, the chief executive of chemicals group Courtaulds, said last week that the rise was bad news for British corporations. "It's obviously bad for UK Plc," he said.
Reams of data pointing to a buoyant British economy, driven by rampant consumer demand, have stoked speculation of interest rate rises and sent yield-hungry investors into pounds.
Sterling's overnight highs represented a rise of nearly 16 percent since August, while its recent four-year peak of $1.6905 marked an increase of more than 12 percent in six months.
Though the pound's strength should dampen inflation in the short term, financial analysts said the Bank of England would not be convinced of the longer-term anti-inflationary effects.
With a general election looming by next May, the analysts said Clarke would not welcome industry complaints.
But the authorities have few weapons with which to combat currency strength, the analysts said.

The dollar's sharp overnight rally -- sparked by remarks from the German Bundesbank (central bank) and the U.S. Federal Reserve about increased buying of dollars ahead of European monetary union -- showed the market's current receptiveness to official comments.
Verbal intervention has its limits, however.

"Talking is difficult -- if you start to talk, the market expects a policy to reflect it. If they're not prepared to back it up with policy action, what can they do?" said Tim Fox, treasury economist at Standard Chartered Bank. The analysts said that with consumers spending increasingly freely, interest rate cuts in Britain were out of the question.

"A sterling rally does take off some of the pressure to raise rates," said Ciaran Barr, economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "But if you were to cut rates that would just add fuel to an already overstoked fire."
